synopsis: Automatic braking can create hazards of its own—operator jolts, shifted or spilled loads, slope instability, rear-end impacts and rollback—and stopping before an object is therefore not a complete safety result [f11877, f2896]. Risk varies by machine and operation, requiring machine-specific hazard analysis and potentially context-dependent braking rather than a universal fastest-stop command; Komatsu specifically requires KomVision to be off during trailer loading because rapid stopping can destabilize the machine [f808, f1977, f1975, f1646]. Validation must address both failure to brake and unsafe or unnecessary braking: shadow mode cannot establish closed-loop secondary effects, whereas branched closed-loop SIL or HIL evaluates stopping distance, clearance and secondary hazards [f5816, f968, f5529]. Most secondary hazards are reported rather than measured: off-road event frequencies and deceleration injury thresholds were not found, worker reports of jolting remain unresolved against MSHA's lack of known injuries, and on-road evidence varies—a reported 20% increase in rear-end strikes contrasts with no collision-producing loss of following distance in the cited Tesla investigation [f11878, f3613, f3612, f3619, f3032, f1503]. Post-stop safety also matters: ISO 21815-3 warns against rollaway when intervention ends and recommends operator action, such as applying the parking brake, before braking is released [f6157, f6158].
